name: Hype Detection Checklist
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Your Hype Detector: A Checklist for Any Big Tech Claim
lesson.summary: After working through quantum computing's real technical state in detail, this chapter hands over a practical, general-purpose checklist for evaluating any hyped technology claim, quantum or otherwise.
lesson.body:
Everything in this course so far has been in service of a specific technical subject, but the real value of working through it carefully is transferable. This chapter turns the critical thinking skills, the moving goalposts pattern, and the unfalsifiable timelines you have already learned to recognize in quantum computing into a checklist you can run against any big technology announcement, in any field, for the rest of your life.

Here are the questions worth asking, every time.

One: what exactly was achieved, in specific measurable terms, versus what is merely claimed will eventually follow from it. "We built a chip with more stable qubits than our previous chip" is a measured claim. "This brings us closer to solving climate change" is a claim about the future wearing the achievement's clothes.

Two: is the timeline for real-world impact specific and falsifiable, like "commercial units shipping by a named date," or vague and unfalsifiable, like "just a few years away" or "on the horizon." Vague timelines cannot be proven wrong, which is exactly why they get repeated for years without anyone having to account for them.

Three: has this organization's timeline moved before, and if the new framing quietly redefines what counts as success compared to the original promise, that is the moving goalposts pattern, and it deserves its own note every time you spot it.

Four: who is making the claim, and do they have a financial or reputational stake in the story being believed, such as an upcoming funding round, a stock price, or a government grant renewal that depends on positive news.

Five: has anyone outside the organization making the claim independently verified it, and can that verification be traced to a specific named source, paper, or replication, rather than an unnamed "expert" or a quote from the same company's own scientists.

Six: is the comparison being made actually fair. A claim like "beats a classical supercomputer" needs a follow-up question: at what specific task, using what specific classical algorithm, and was that the best classical approach available, or a weaker one chosen because it was easier to beat.

Seven: what would have to be true for this claim to be false, and is that a test anyone could actually run. If no observation or result could ever count as evidence against the claim, the claim is not really making a testable prediction at all.

None of these questions, on their own, prove a claim is false. Extraordinary claims are sometimes simply true, and asking hard questions is not the same as assuming bad faith. But the more of these questions go unanswered or get actively dodged, the more scrutiny the claim has earned before you repeat it as settled fact. This checklist works the same way whether the claim is about quantum computers, a new AI model, a battery technology, a biotech breakthrough, or the next big thing nobody has announced yet.
